questions.question: Explain the mechanism of F ⁺ –F ⁻ conjugation in bacteria. What is the role of the F plasmid in this process? / [CO1, CO2, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the mechanism of F+ to F- conjugation in bacteria. What is the role of the F plasmid
  • in this process [U] [CO2]
  • Mechanism of F+ to F- Conjugation: An F+ (donor) cell extends a sex pilus and attaches to an
  • F- (recipient) cell, forming a conjugation canal and enabling plasmid mobilisation [2]. Rolling
  • circle replication occurs, and the recipient cell becomes an F+ cell, now capable of acting as a
  • donor [1]. Role of F Plasmid- Carries tra genes to form the sex pilus and initiate transfer . It is
  • the DNA molecule transferred, making the recipient a new donor . [2]

questions.question: Explain the mechanism by which gamma rays cause DNA mutations. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the mechanism by which gamma rays cause DNA mutations. [U] [CO3]
  • Gamma rays are a form of ionising radiation.[1]. They cause double-stranded breaks in the
  • DNA backbone.[2]. The cell's repair mechanisms are error-prone, leading to deletions,
  • insertions, or chromosomal rearrangements.[2]

  • region.[1]. The central region contains additional genes (e.g., for antibiotic resistance).[1]. The
  • two IS elements can be in direct or inverted repeat orientation [1]. The IS elements provide
  • the transposase enzyme needed for movement [1]. Any Example: Tn 10 (confers tetracycline
  • resistance), flanked by two IS10 elements.[1]

questions.question: Illustrate the sequence of events that occur when E. coli is transferred from a glucose-rich medium to a lactose-only medium. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Illustrate the sequence of events that occur when E.coli is transferred from a glucose-rich
  • medium to a lactose–only medium [U] [CO2]
  • Glucose is depleted. cAMP levels rise and bind to CAP(CRP), activating it [ 1]. The lac
  • repressor is inactivated by binding to the inducer (lactose) [1]. The cAMP-CRP complex binds
  • to the promoter region, thereby enhancing RNA polymerase binding. Transcription of the lac
  • operon (lacZ, lacY , lacA genes) occurs. Translation produces the enzymes β-galactosidase
  • (metabolises lactose) and lactose permease (transports lactose). [2]. Diagram [1]

questions.question: What are the applications of plasmids? / [CO1, CO2, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What are the applications of plasmids? [K]/[CO1]
  • Introduction to plasmids [3]. Seven applications include: Cloning: Serve as vectors to insert and
  • replicate foreign DNA in a host cell. Protein Production: Used to express large quantities of
  • recombinant proteins (e.g., insulin, vaccines). Gene Therapy: Acts as a vector to deliver therapeutic
  • genes to human cells. Used to study gene function and regulation in molecular biology. Antibiotic
  • Resistance Markers: Enable the selection of successfully transformed bacteria. Synthetic
  • Biology: Act as standardised pa rts to build novel genetic circuits. DNA Sequencing. Gene
  • Knockdown: Basis for constructing plasmids for RNA interference. Bioremediation. Used to create
  • genetically modified (GM) crops with desirable traits.[7]
